title: Nekuda, sefira, partzuf: why the essential points of Tohu break, and how Tikun makes a person
overview:
Before the ten *sefiros* of *Atzilus*, the chapter brings in *nekuda*, *sefira* and *partzuf*: the difference between *Tohu* and *Tikun*. In *Tohu* each *sefira* is a point, the essence of an attribute before it spreads: a will for kindness that has a definition but no reason and no particular ways, like a person who is kind by nature, not one who read Dale Carnegie. Even its intellect and its *netzach* are the same point, all in one vessel, the *Akudim*.

So the *sefiros* of *Tohu* cannot join: two opposite essential goals allow no compromise, and whoever makes one of them the cure-all, "totally nice, always" or "get it yourself", fails. *Tikun* is the will for how to reach the goal. Kindness then depends on a reason, and one thing can be loved and hated at once, as G-d punished Shaul and ordered his eulogy at the same time. Only *Tikun* makes a *partzuf*, a person who sees the goal both sides share and takes the practical step, the way G-d mixed fire and water.

terms.gloss: the world of Chaos: each sefira only a point, an essential goal that cannot join its opposite
the world of Repair: each sefira divided into ten, so that they work together in harmony; the will for how to reach the goal
a point: the essence of an attribute before it spreads out, a bias with no reason and no particular ways
inclusion: the attributes working together like a harmony
the Name of forty-five: the abstract that a concrete form, BaN, comes to express
the Name of fifty-two: the concrete form, a vessel or an angel, that represents the abstract MaH
the bound ones: all ten sefiros included in one vessel, all one point
here: the point of Tohu even when divided into ten, each still a point, with no inclusion
lit. face: the stature of a person, the inclusion of all opposites; only in Tikun
composite kindness: kindness that depends on a reason, such as to one who did you a favor, weighed out by the situation
a middle: the place a thing loved from one side and hated from another ends up on one's list
a person of daas, who explains each of two opposite views better than its holder and finds the goal they share

sections.title: Before the sefiros of Atzilus: nekuda, sefira, partzuf, and the difference between Tohu and Tikun
sections.summary: Before the ten *sefiros* of *Atzilus* are explained one by one, the chapter brings in the three stages *nekuda*, *sefira* and *partzuf*. In *Tohu* each *sefira* is only a point; in *Tikun* each is divided into ten, and so they work together in harmony, through the Name *MaH*.

phrases.he: (כ) והנה קודם שיבואר ענין פרטי העשר ספירות דאצילות יש להקדים ענין נקודה ספירה פרצוף כו'
דהיות ידוע ההפרש שבין בחינת התהו לבחינת התיקון בכלל,
דעשר ספירות דתהו הן בבחינת נקודות לבד,
phrases.en: In *Tohu*, each *sefira* is like a *nekuda*.

phrases.he: שהן בבחינת הכתרים

blocks.text: Now he starts on *Keser* (crown). First the chapter explains the general *inyan* (matter) of *nekudos*, *sefira* and *partzuf* (points, a single attribute, and a full stature of attributes), and of *Tikun* and *Tohu* (the worlds of Repair and of Chaos), to understand how the *igulim* (circles) of *Atzilus* relate to its *yosher* (the straight line).

**In *Tohu*, each *sefira* is like a *nekuda*** (a point): it is not yet ten. As the last chapter explained, the association of your *etzem ratzon* (essential will) with something makes a bias, a leaning towards *chesed* (kindness) or another way. The leaning is just a point, not yet an actual, particular will for *chesed* or anything else. But it is the general thing, the source of every particular that comes out afterwards.

phrases.he: ובעולם התיקון הוא בבחינת התחלקות כל ספירה לי',
phrases.en: And then in *Tikun*, each *sefira* becomes already divided to ten.

phrases.he: על כן ממילא נעשה בחינת התיקון
phrases.en: and since each *sefira* is now diverse, it automatically makes it *Tikun*.

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת ההתכללות
phrases.en: That's the idea of *hiskalelus*, that it's like a harmony.

phrases.he: על ידי שם מ''ה כו'

blocks.text: In *Tikun* each *sefira* is already divided into ten, and because each is now diverse, that automatically makes it *Tikun*. *Tikun* has many senses; here it means a harmony, the things working together. That is *hiskalelus* (inclusion): **it's like a harmony**.

The harmony comes through the Name *MaH* (the Name of forty-five). *MaH* and *BaN* always relate the same way: when something concrete with a set form, a *kli* (vessel) or an angel, can represent something abstract, the abstract is *MaH* and the *kli* is *BaN*.

blocks.title: Letters make a vessel for an idea
blocks.text: Language, for example. The words are a tangible form, but by putting a whole bunch of letters in different orders you make a *kli* in which an abstract idea can be expressed.

sections.title: The point: the essence of a midda before it spreads, a will for kindness with no reason
sections.summary: The *nekuda* is the essence of an attribute before it spreads out. It is not the essence as it is in the *yechida*, but the will for kindness once it is revealed: it already has a definition, but no reason and no particular ways of coming out.

phrases.he: וביאור הדברים ידוע שבחינת הנקודות הוא בחינת העצמיות טרם שמתפשט,
phrases.en: The *nekudos* is like the *etzem* before it spreads out,

phrases.he: כנקודה שהיא בלתי מתפשטת כו'
phrases.en: like a *nekuda* that doesn't come out yet.

blocks.text: The *nekudos* are the *etzem* (essence) before it spreads out. As the *igulim* are the soul before it comes into the body and the *yosher* the soul coming into it, so *Tohu* and *Tikun* are the way it is in the *etzem* and the way it comes out, the *hispashtus* (spreading forth). The point is **like a *nekuda* that doesn't come out yet**, still within its *etzem hiyuli* (the raw, formless essence).

phrases.he: כמו אור מדת החסד,
phrases.en: for example, *chesed*,

phrases.he: הנה בחינת עצמיות דמדת החסד הוא בחינת הכתר שלו

blocks.text: Take, **for example, *chesed***: the essence of the attribute is its *Keser*. The *etzem* of the *midda* (attribute) of kindness is a desire for kindness, so that a person always leans to do things in a nice way.

phrases.he: ואמנם אין הכוונה על בחינת העצמיות דמדת החסד כמו שהוא נטוע ומושרש בעצם הנפש שנקרא יחידה
phrases.en: But we're not talking here about the *etzem* like it is in the *yechida*,

phrases.he: כנזכר לעיל, שהוא בחינת היולי לגמרי (כנזכר לעיל באות יו''ד וי''א)
אלא הכוונה הוא על בחינת גלוי הרצון לדבר חסד פרטי
phrases.en: We're talking about now when a person has a particular *ratzon* for doing an actual kind thing.

phrases.he: מן העלם חסד העצמיות ההיולי

blocks.text: Not the essence of *chesed* as it is planted and rooted in the essence of the soul, the *yechida*, where it is entirely *hiyuli* (raw potential); that corresponds to before the *tzimtzum* (contraction), as was said in chapters 10 and 11.

It is the will for a particular act of *chesed*, revealed out of the hidden kindness of the essence. The essential *chesed* made a *ratzon* (will) to be a nice person; *Adam Kadmon* makes it a picture of what a nice person is; and the picture now yields particular *ratzonos* (wills) to do nice things.

Yet all those particular kind acts still share one *nekuda*, that he sees them as nice: the essence comes over into them. Through *Adam Kadmon* *chesed* has a form now, "you can look it up in a dictionary what *chesed* is", but the point, wanting whatever is nice, is still there.

phrases.he: שגם זה הרצון
phrases.en: even this particular *ratzon*, that you want to do a nice thing,

phrases.he: הוא בלתי התפשטות עדיין
רק כמו שהוא בלא טעם כלל
phrases.en: this is without any reason at all,

phrases.he: לרצון זה, למה רוצה בגלוי לחסד זה כו'
ומכל שכן שאין בו בחינת התחלקות אופנים שונים
phrases.en: and he definitely didn't yet think up particular ways of exactly what he wants to do.

blocks.text: Even this will to do nice things is still without *hispashtus*. He knows what being nice means, but has nothing particular yet; the situation will decide what comes out. Like a nice person: he leans towards kindness, but right now nothing is coming up, so he is not doing anything.

And **this is without any reason at all**. He does not want it in order to reach some goal in a given situation; the *chesed* is the goal. That is his *etzem*, the *nekuda*: he likes it because of who he is.

blocks.title: Dale Carnegie's book
blocks.text: It is not like someone who is nice to people because he read Dale Carnegie's *How to Win Friends and Influence People* and knows a career needs it. Being nice is not his *ratzon*: "the *nekuda* of their *ratzon* is to make money, or whatever it is."

But a person whose nature is *chafetz chesed* (desires kindness) builds a self-image of a kind person, and being kind and caring is his goal in life, or part of it. Having such an *Adam Kadmon* gives him a constant *nekuda*: he wants to do kind things.

All the more it has no division into separate ways. Since he is not doing it as a means to an end, he **definitely didn't yet think up particular ways of exactly what he wants to do**. He has no will for doing such and such, only for whatever will be kind.

blocks.title: A will for money, from any deal
blocks.text: Likewise someone with an *etzem ratzon* for money does not care how it comes, from this deal or that; he just wants the money. So too here: he wants the *chesed*, and does not care how it comes out.

sections.title: Intellect and victory inside the point: all one point, the Akudim in one vessel
sections.summary: Even the bias of the intellect towards kindness, the *chachma* of that *chesed*, and its *netzach* are only the same point. The ten are there, but with no recognizable division: this is the world of *Akudim*, all in one *kli*.

phrases.he: או גם אם שכלו מטה כלפי חסד דווקא, אין בו התחלקות אופנים שונים
אף על פי ששכל הנוטה בעצם לחסד ולזכות, הוא בחינת חכמה שבחסד העצמי, אבל גם הוא רק בבחינת נקודה

blocks.question: "Wait a minute": if his essential will biases his intellect towards kindness, is that not *chachma*, a division already within the point?
blocks.text: That too is a *nekuda*, not an actual *sechel* (intellect) yet. His *sechel* will always lean to being liberal and kind, to looking at things with a good eye; but the leaning is part of the same point, with no division into different ways.

His intellect leaning to kindness and merit is the *chachma* (wisdom) of the essential *chesed*, but only a point. Everything, even in *Tohu*, divides ten within ten, so a *chachma* is there. But it is the same *nekuda*, that he wants *chesed*: his *chachma* wants *chesed*, his *middos* (emotional attributes) want *chesed*. It is a point because it has nothing yet to do with a particular situation; whatever comes up, he already leans this way.

phrases.he: וכן נצח שבחסד זה
phrases.en: that he's going to want to overcome any opposition to any *chesed*.

phrases.he: הוא בא בבחינת נקודה
ונמצא דגם שבחינת החסד העצמי הבא בגלוי כלול מי', רצון ושכל ומדות, אבל אין בהם התחלקות ניכרת
phrases.en: even though really, technically, it does have ten, you could divide it up into ten *sefiros*, there's no recognizable distinction

phrases.he: אלא כולן בבחינת נקודה אחד,
phrases.en: they're all in one *nekuda*,

phrases.he: והוא בחינת העקודים, שעקודים היו בכלי אחד כו'
phrases.en: This is the level of *Akudim*, where really all of the ten *sefiros* are included in one *kli*,

blocks.text: So too the *netzach* (victory) of this *chesed*: **that he's going to want to overcome any opposition to any *chesed***. He has not yet found anything in his way, but if something were, he would fight it. It is a point halfway, and it too comes as a point.

So the essential *chesed* coming into the open includes all ten, will, intellect and *middos*, with no recognizable division. Technically you could divide it into ten *sefiros*, but they are all the same *nekuda*: he wants *chesed*, and everything together goes to *chesed*.

Rather, **they're all in one *nekuda***. **This is the level of *Akudim***, the bound ones: all ten *sefiros* in one *kli*. His *ratzon*, *sechel* and *middos* right now all mean the same thing, that he wants *chesed*, and it does not matter which one you name. It is just his final goal.

sections.title: Sefira: the sefiros of Tohu cannot join, and two opposite goals cannot compromise
sections.summary: Because each *sefira* of *Tohu* is an essential goal, they cannot unite: one reigns and dies, then the next. Two opposite essential wills cannot be mixed or compromised, and a person or a society that makes one of them the cure-all fails; so too Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel could not convince each other.

phrases.he: ולזה בחינת עשר ספירות דתהו הן בלתי מתיחדין ומתכללין זה עם זה
phrases.en: And therefore the *sefiros* of *Tohu* do not unite or include with each other at all,

phrases.he: אלא הן זה תחת זה
phrases.en: they're one under the other,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב וימלוך וימת כו'

blocks.text: So the ten *sefiros* of *Tohu* do not unite or include each other at all. They are one under the other, as it says of each king of *Tohu*, "and he reigned, and he died": the kings of Esav, who represent the kings of *Tohu*.

phrases.he: כמו רצון העצמי שבא בגלוי חסד
הגם שכלול בו שכל כו', לא יתחבר עם רצון עצמי היפוכו הבא בבחינת הדין

blocks.text: So the essential will that comes out as *chesed*, though intellect is included in it, will not join with the opposite essential will, which comes as *din* (judgement). You see it very much in politics: for whatever reason, one person has liberal leanings, another conservative.
You see it in anything people believe in: it is really a belief, an *etzem nekuda* they are connected to, like people with missionaries and the like. They believe whatever it is.

sensitivity.reason: Holds up missionaries as the type of believer whose reasoning is only a front for a fixed belief.
sensitivity.publishable: You see it in anything people believe in: it is really a belief, an *etzem nekuda* they are connected to. They believe whatever it is.

blocks.text: So both sides will come into *sechel* to try to convince you, but it is not really *sechel*; it is *ratzon*, still their belief. "You could talk to one of these guys till you're blue" and never convince him, because it is a one-way *sechel*: "*sechel*'s a puppet to convince you of what they believe."

That is not necessarily bad; this is how it starts. On this level, that is what *sechel* was built for: to interpret and express to somebody else what you believe. But it cannot convince someone whose *etzem nekuda* is somewhere else.
This is also why, whenever you come to a thing like this, like in Israel with the Jews and the Arabs, because it is a religious thing, democracy does not work.

You cannot tell two people to sit down and compromise if their inner goals conflict. On things that serve the goal you can compromise: we want different things, but find something to our mutual benefit, so we both gain. On the goal itself there is no room, because "my *etzem ratzon* is exact opposite of your *etzem ratzon*."

But what if the issue is the thing itself, one guy's life against the other's? You cannot say, "Well, make a compromise." "It's an all-or-nothing deal." So too within a person: of these essential wills he can really have only one at a time.

blocks.title: Totally nice, always
blocks.text: Some people live in *Tohu*, in the *igulim*. They lock on to *chesed*: "That's it, I'm going to be totally nice always." Without a mature view they do not realize that sometimes, to accomplish *chesed*, you must do something outwardly *gevura* (might, restraint), even when *chesed* is the real goal; that is the *inyan* of *Tikun*. So they try to be altruistically nice all the time, and get stepped on. Try it with a country or a classroom: eventually it fails, and so it dies.

blocks.title: "Get it yourself"
blocks.text:
Then he says, "Oh, so now I'm going to do *gevura*," also in the way of *Tohu*. Anybody asks him to pass the salt: "Get it yourself." There is a *maala* (an advantage) in making people work, but "only get what you deserve" does not work either, and so that also dies.

So with every one of them: a person or a society that makes one the cure-all fails. And only one is possible at a time, because in their essence they contradict each other.

phrases.he: (כמחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל וכהאי גוונא,
דגם שמנגדו יקשה עליו
phrases.en: even if the opposition will ask questions to him,

phrases.he: ולא יוכל למצוא טעם
phrases.en: and he's not able to find an explanation,

phrases.he: ישתוק,
phrases.en: he'll be quiet,

phrases.he: אבל לא יוכל להודות ולחזור בו,
phrases.en: he's not able to admit and then change his mind,

phrases.he: להתכלל בדעה שמנגדו כלל כו')
phrases.en: to the opposite opinion at all.

blocks.text: Like the dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel. Why did they not convince each other? They were reasonable people. Because their dispute came from an essential difference, from the root of their souls, not from *sechel*: a *Tohu* kind of thing. But they were in holiness, which is why this is in parentheses: it is not a full example.

Once the *halacha* (the law) was decided, Beis Shammai did like Beis Hillel, or Beis Hillel like Beis Shammai, whichever way it went. By their essential leaning they were biased to see and deal with things a certain way, but their connection to Torah was deeper: if the Torah says to do it like this, they would, even if they did not see it that way.

So **even if the opposition will ask questions to him**, and **he's not able to find an explanation, he'll be quiet**: "I don't know." But he cannot turn back on his opinion, because it is not based on logic; he perceives things that way, and the *sechel* is just looking for the right words. That is how it works in Torah: they perceive it in spirituality, then look for words to bring it into human intellect, which is not its root.

But **he's not able to admit and then change his mind** and agree **to the opposite opinion at all**. Each has a point that is essential, and *eilu v'eilu divrei Elokim chaim* ("these and these are the words of the living G-d"), so there is no reason to concede.

sections.title: Tikun: the midda spreads out of its essence, into a will for how to reach the goal
sections.summary: In *Tikun* the attribute comes out of its point: it is no longer about the goal but about how to accomplish it in a particular case. Then kindness depends on a reason, like kindness to one who did you a favor, and it is a composite kindness; so too the composite judgement of a kind man toward his enemy.

phrases.he: אבל בחינת התיקון היינו כאשר המדה בא מבחינת נקודה שלה להתפשטות חוץ מן העצמיות רצון ושכל שבה

blocks.text: *Tikun* is when the *midda* comes out of its point into *hispashtus*, outside its essence, will and intellect. Now we are not talking about your *etzem ratzon*, your goal: "Okay, whatever your goal is, forget about the goal." Now we are talking about how to accomplish it.

Your essential goal is the thing of religion. Religion is about ultimate truths, the ultimate reality and the ultimate goal of a person and of the world, so there can only be one truth: "you can't have pluralism in religion."

blocks.title: Going to New York by way of the south
blocks.text: The means are another matter. Traveling, you have to know your destination, and that you cannot change: if you are going to New York, you cannot be going to Chicago, you have to pick. But sometimes, to get somewhere north, you have to go south, around something. That is a whole separate *ratzon*. Whoever just starts walking in that direction will come up against all these walls in his way.

blocks.title: The short long way and the long short way
blocks.text: Like the story of the long short way and the short long way. The guy wants to get to the palace. Going straight, the short long way, he ends up very close, but there is a wall in front of him and he cannot get in: short, but long. The long short way compromises and goes slowly, but it is short, because you actually get there. "Shortcuts make for long delays"; clever schemes with these things are not worth it.
So this is the *inyan* of *Tikun*: we are no longer dealing with the *etzem ratzon*, but with the *ratzon* for how to accomplish it in a particular instance.

phrases.he: דהיינו כמו מדת החסד כאשר יולד הרצון ושכל להטות כלפי חסד לזולתו
מצד שעשה לו טובה
phrases.en: You want to be nice to somebody because he did you a favor.

phrases.he: ולא מצד בחינת עצם הטוב הבא בגלוי בהכרח מטבע הטוב שבעצמיות נפשו
אדרבה יוכל להיות אכזרי בטבע,
phrases.en: The person could be cruel naturally.

phrases.he: ולמי שחננו והצילו ממות
phrases.en: But to somebody that saved his life, that did a lot of kindness to him and saved his life,

phrases.he: וכהאי גוונא
ירצה להטיב,
phrases.en: for that person he's going to always be gracious,

phrases.he: ויטה שכלו עליו תמיד לחסד וזכות
phrases.en: and he's always going to be biased to look at them favorably.

phrases.he: כו' וכהאי גוונא

blocks.text: For example *chesed*, when the will and intellect to lean towards kindness to another are born because he did him a favor. Not that in your essence you always want to be kind to everybody: **You want to be nice to somebody because he did you a favor.**

Say he wants his personal happiness, or money. If a guy helps him out, he will be kind to him, the *sechel* being that it will help him more in the future; or maybe he just has an essential gratitude. But he does not act this way to everybody. It depends what the person does: be nice to people who are nice to you, and not to people who are not.

And not from the essential kindness that comes out necessarily from the good nature of his soul. From the essential *chesed* he would have to be nice to everybody, because that is his nature, whatever the person did to him or not.

On the contrary, **the person could be cruel naturally**. **But to somebody that saved his life, that did a lot of kindness to him**, **he's going to always be gracious**, **and he's always going to be biased to look at them favorably**. He has connected his *etzem ratzon* to that person as much as the person did for him: the more kindness, the more connection. Now it gets complicated: when are you nice and when not? This is the *ratzon murkav* (the composite will).

phrases.he: שזה נקרא חסד וטוב המורכב,
phrases.en: this is called a complex or composite kindness and good.

phrases.he: ולא חסד פשוט ועצמי
phrases.en: it's not the same simple thing for everybody

phrases.he: שמצד הטבע כלל
וכהאי גוונא יובן בהיפוכו,
phrases.en: the same way with the opposite,

phrases.he: במדת הדין המורכב, להטות רצונו ושכלו כלפי חוב לשונאו שעשה לו רעה הרבה,
גם שבעצם טבעו הוא איש חסדן ורחמן כו'
phrases.en: even if *b'etzem* he's a kind person,

blocks.text: This is **a complex or composite kindness and good**, *chesed hamurkav*: it has many parts, and you have to weigh the situation. It is not a simple, essential *chesed* coming from nature; **it's not the same simple thing for everybody**.

The same with the opposite, the composite attribute of judgement: bending his will and intellect against an enemy and hater who did him much harm. Somebody very mean to him becomes his enemy. That does not make him a cruel guy, **even if *b'etzem* he's a kind person**, compassionate: by nature he likes to be kind, but he has to realize there are certain people you should not be nice to.

Had he made *chesed* his whole *metzius* (existence), he could say, "Well, even if I'm gonna get killed for it, I'm going to be nice to somebody, even if it's gonna bite me back." But at the *pnimiyus* (the inner side), even within *Tohu* there is the head, the inner will they come from; so *Tikun* has a higher *shoresh* (root).

blocks.title: The parent who wants to be loved
blocks.text: A parent who wants a relationship of love with his kids is outwardly kind so they will appreciate and love him back. He does what the kids will see as kind, and that does not mean he really wants to be kind. Go deeper: the inner will to be kind is for their benefit. If you really want that, you will be willing to do what outwardly looks like *gevura*, depending on the *sechel*.

sections.title: In the composite, opposites can live together: love and hate, Shaul, Shlomo and the Flood
sections.summary: Once the attributes are tied to a thing through a reason, one thing can be loved from one side and hated from another, and a middle is weighed out between them. So G-d punished and honored Shaul at once, was angry and joyful over Shlomo, and found in man's evil inclination both a reason to destroy and a reason to spare: in *Tikun*, in the actual world, nothing is pure.

phrases.he: ועל דרך זה יובן שיוכל להיות במורכב כמה מיני אופנים שונים
phrases.en: once you start having these considerations, it can come out in many different ways

phrases.he: מאד, לפי אופן דבר שמורכב בו המדות
phrases.en: according to the considerations that you're using to put together the *middos*.

phrases.he: כמו אהבה ושנאה
התלויים בדבר
phrases.en: that are dependent on something,

phrases.he: כנזכר לעיל
הרי יוכל למצוא דבר שמצדו א' יאהבנו, ויהיה רצונו ושכלו הכל לטוב וחסד, ומצדו הב' באותו הדבר עצמו, ישנאנו ויטה רצונו ושכלו לרע ועונש

blocks.text: So the composite can come in very different ways: **once you start having these considerations, it can come out in many different ways**, **according to the considerations that you're using to put together the *middos***. Like love and hate **that are dependent on something**: one and the same thing he can love from one side, his will and intellect all for good and kindness, and hate from another, leaning to bad and punishment.
Once your essential *middos* hang on something through a *sechel*, it can be good for me by one consideration and bad for me by another: from this side I love it, from that side I hate it.

blocks.title: Drugs and their side effects
blocks.text: Drugs, for example. People like them because they are pleasurable and feel good, and hate them for what they do to them, the side effects. They love the positive and hate the negative, but since it is one actual thing in the world, both are connected to it: you cannot have one without the other.

With both tied to the one thing, your *sechel* associates two opposite *middos* with it, liking it from this side and hating it from that, and you have to decide which overrides the other in practice, and how to act.

phrases.he: עד שיוכל להיות בחינת ממוצע
phrases.en: until you come out with a *memutza*

phrases.he: כלול מחסד וגבורה יחד

blocks.text: Until there can be a *memutza* (a middle), including *chesed* and *gevura* together. Essentially there is no mixing: what you like you totally like, what you hate you totally hate. But practically you can prioritize: "this is going to end up on my list of things that I like somewhere in the middle, because on the one hand I like it, but on the other hand it's bad."

blocks.title: Profit and expenses in a business deal
blocks.text: But in an actual physical thing both come together, so you can do a simple equation: measure the pleasure against the pain, subtract, and maximize. Like a business deal: you want the profit and not the expenses. A deal may bring in some money but cost more than it gains, so it is not worth it; or you gain a little; or you gain a lot.

blocks.title: Only a deal that is profitable enough
blocks.text: The money coming back is always what you want. But acting by *sechel*, you only do a deal profitable enough to meet your needs, not "any deal that's going to end up making somebody give me money." So you make a hierarchy, this better than that, and a *memutza*: this one is "so-so."

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב באשר משפטו שם כו'
על שאול שהמית את הגבעונים ועל שלא נספד כהלכה,
דבר והיפוכו כאחד

blocks.text: As it is written, *ba'asher mishpato sham* ("I forget how the end of the word is"): where *Hashem* judges, there you find His compassion and His *chesed*. It seems like opposite things.

blocks.title: Shaul punished and eulogized
blocks.text: This was said of Shaul, who killed the Givonim and was not eulogized as he should have been: one thing and its opposite at once. Because Shaul killed the Givonim, who had helped Dovid, there was a plague; through prophecy they found it was because of Shaul, and Dovid gave over some of Shaul's descendants to the Givonim to be hung. That was Shaul's punishment. At the same time Dovid was told to make a *hesped* (eulogy) for Shaul, because he had never been given proper honor.

So is G-d mad at Shaul or happy with him? He punishes and rewards him at once. It was not an essential thing, that He hates Shaul and that's it, or likes him. A parent who yells at a child for doing wrong still loves him: "what you do good I like, and what you don't do good I don't like." The two are not connected, so both can be at once.

phrases.he: וכן כשנשא שלמה בת פרעה,
phrases.en: also with *Shlomo*, that *Hashem* was angry because he married *Bas Paroh*,

phrases.he: על זה אמר כי על אפי כו'
phrases.en: that this is: I'm angry,

phrases.he: ושיר השירים נאמר על שמחת בנין בית המקדש
וכמו שכתוב ביום שמחת לבו כו'
phrases.en: the day of the rejoicing of his heart, which is the time the *Beis HaMikdash* was built,

phrases.he: שמחה וחרון אף, דבר והיפוכו כאחד
phrases.en: So we see that *Hashem* both had *simcha* and anger at *Shlomo* at the same time.

blocks.text: So too Shlomo. *Hashem* was angry that he married *Bas Paroh* (Pharaoh's daughter): *ki al api*, "**I'm angry**", angry about it forever. Yet *Shir HaShirim* (the Song of Songs) was said on the joy of building the *Beis HaMikdash* (the Temple), a whole song of *simcha* (joy) and of how much *Hashem* loved Shlomo: "on the day of the rejoicing of his heart", the day it was built. Joy and burning anger, one thing and its opposite at once.

phrases.he: וכן כי יצר לב האדם רע וכו'
phrases.en: and the same thing with man

phrases.he: ומתחלה אמר וירא יהו״ה כי רבה רעת האדם כו' וינחם כו'
phrases.en: First, before the flood, it says G-d saw how bad man was, and He regretted making man.

blocks.text: And **the same thing with man**. Before the *Mabul* (the Flood) G-d said: since man is bad, we will destroy him. After it He said: since man is bad, we will not destroy him. The same fact, that man has a *yetzer hara* (evil inclination), was a reason both to hate him and to have mercy on him.

blocks.title: Both sides of a court case
blocks.text: One side says, "Well, they're bad, we should get rid of them." The other: "Yeah, but they're born bad, so it's not their fault." It is like a court case, where each side shows how the same *nekuda* connects to *chesed* or to *gevura*. "They're born bad, so they're going to sin." "Then it's not their fault, so be easy on them." "No, that makes them worse. That means there's even no hope." It just depends: "Whatever you want, you'll be able to use that as an excuse for it."

blocks.title: Why the rainbow came after the Flood
blocks.text: In the end, before the *Mabul* the bad could not be refined; after it the world was refined a little, which is why there can be a rainbow. In a rainbow the cloud obstructs the light. Before, the atmosphere was too thick; after, it was thinner, so the light came through and, hitting the raindrops, made a rainbow, revealing the hidden beauty in the light through that resistance.

blocks.title: Why the rainbow came after the Flood
blocks.text: So after the *Mabul* a person's bad was refined enough to be used for good: he can overcome his *yetzer hara*, and the very fight, the difficulty of doing what G-d wants, brings out the inner beauty of his connection to G-d, of his *nefesh Elokis* (G-dly soul). Before the *Mabul* it could not be used that way, so the bad side won.
And at first, before the *Mabul*, it says that G-d saw how bad man was, and He regretted making man.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב במקום אחר
שזהו מבחינת המדות דתיקון,
phrases.en: the fact that you can have both *middos* for the same thing is because it's in *Tikun*,

phrases.he: שהם בבחינת מורכבים
phrases.en: which are complex.

phrases.he: דהיינו בהתפשטות דבר
phrases.en: that you're dealing not with a theory.

phrases.he: שלא מצד העצמיות לבד
על כן יוכל להיות התכללות דבר והיפוכו כו'
phrases.en: Therefore, you can have two opposite things,

blocks.text: As explained in a *maamar* (discourse), this is from the *middos* of *Tikun*: **the fact that you can have both *middos* for the same thing is because it's in *Tikun***, where they are composite, in the *hispashtus* of the thing. In theory things can be pure; in practice nothing is. Everything has a benefit and a detriment, and no physical thing is completely pleasurable or completely painful.

blocks.title: All the powers of the soul in one body
blocks.text: In the *hispashtus*, the physical world, everything comes together. As when the soul comes into the body: the body separates each power, yet seeing, hearing and all the powers of the soul are connected in one body. So any physical thing has all the *sefiros* and *middos* in one, in different proportions, so that it is not found as only itself alone.

blocks.title: No light without a little darkness
blocks.text: **Therefore, you can have two opposite things**, one thing and its opposite together. In theory light and darkness, or sweet and bitter, are complete opposites, each contradicting the other. In practice you never find anything that is not a mixture of both. There is no pure light that is only bright: you could always make it brighter, which means there is a little darkness there.

sections.title: Tohu stays a sefira; only Tikun makes a partzuf, a person, like fire and water mixed
sections.summary: Even divided into ten, the point of *Tohu* is only a *sefira*, not the *partzuf* of a person who includes all opposites. A person, and *Tikun*, sees the deeper goal both sides share and works it out in practice, without dropping the goal; as *Sefer Yetzira* says, G-d mixed fire and water, not in their essence but as composites.

phrases.he: והיינו בחינת נקודה דתהו,
דגם כשנעשה בהתחלקות לי', אין זה רק ספירה
phrases.en: Even in *Tohu*, when it divides up into a *sefira*, and it has ten *sefiros*, they're also *nekudos*.

blocks.text: This is the point of *Tohu*, the essential *middos*: *Akudim*, one point. **Even in *Tohu*, when it divides up into a *sefira*, and it has ten *sefiros*, they're also *nekudos***, so it is not really *hiskalelus*. In *Tohu* the *gevura* is really all *chesed*, all one *sefira*: the *chesed* takes the *gevura* and makes it a *chesed* too.

blocks.title: Even more reason to be nice to him
blocks.text: Like the guys who lean towards *chesed*. Tell them, "Well, this guy is so bad, look at all the bad things he did," and they say, "Oh, so that's even more of a reason that we should be nice to him. Poor person," he's a victim and everything. They turn anything into a *chesed*.

Because it is a *sefira*: a guy who in his essence believes or wants a certain way, from his *emuna* (faith) or his will. He may come and talk to you deliberately, even go out to missionize, like the *Akudim* of *Tohu*; but it is still only one *sefira*. He is not considering the other side at all.

You see the sign of it a lot. A person in the way of *Tohu* tries to make his whole *partzuf* out of one *sefira*. But the real *etzem* includes all ten, and he should be able to have them all together. One who cannot shows a very big *shtarkeit* (fierceness), a fierce opposition to the opposite, because he feels it threatens his *inyan*.

*Tikun* needs a deeper look; the next chapter explains the middle *kav* (line), which connects opposites. Take two opposite opinions: the *chesed* guy vehemently opposes the *gevura* side, the *gevura* guy vehemently opposes the *chesed* view, and each sees the other as "completely evil and wrong and subversive and everything."

But a *bar daas* (a person of *daas*), as the Frierdiker Rebbe (the previous Lubavitcher Rebbe) describes *daas* (knowledge) in a *maamar*, takes the two and says, "I'm going to explain to both of you what your view is, better than you understand it." He peels it off to the real depth: you do not really want a particular instance of *chesed*. He shows them the real *etzem ratzon* of *chesed*, before it is tied to a certain deed, and brings it up a step.

Up a step, you ask: why do you really want *chesed*? What is the theory behind it? "Every person has in them a little bit of good," and you lean towards letting him off because you appreciate that good and want to bring it out, to be expressed. That is the main *nekuda*, and brought out, it will help him and other people.

And *gevura* says, "It doesn't matter what's inside, that he means well or he has potential. If it doesn't come out into deed, then it's worthless." So he says, "Well, really you both want the same thing": that the inner good come out and be expressed externally. Now decide the best way to get there: "What is the best way to get this person to bring out his inner good?"

By telling him he is really good, that we love him and appreciate his value as a person? Or by being strict, telling him he is not doing good enough and we expect more of him? It depends on the person, on his nature. So you are willing to do whatever it is: for your real goal it does not matter which one you do, only which one works.

blocks.title: Live and let live, or sit down together
blocks.text: To get the *middos* of *Tohu* really into *Tikun*: there is a *Tikun* after a *midda* of *Tohu* that is like a *reshus harabim* (a public domain), kind of like in America. Everybody keeps his own *ratzon* and its opposites; we just make sure people do not go around killing those with opposite views, and they relate in things that do not touch their essential will.

But a real *Tikun* means two people actually sit down and work together. For that you have to find their real, deeper goal, a common goal that transcends both of their particulars. In *Tohu*, though, even when it comes out, it only becomes a *sefira*, not a *partzuf*.

phrases.he: ולא פרצוף אדם,
phrases.en: It's not a person.

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת ההתכללות מכל ההפכים כו'

blocks.text: Not the *partzuf* of a person. It is not a person: you are talking to a wall still. The *inyan* of a person is the inclusion of all opposites.

You see this a lot with *baalei teshuva* (returnees to Judaism). Without proper instruction it is very easy for them to end up not being a person. Their whole approach to religion is *emuna*, with a passionate drive for altruism; connect that to one aspect of the truth and they become forcefully attached to it, and "they're not going to be human." You cannot sit down and talk to them: "they're on a holy mission," and "if you try to talk to them, they're not there."

sensitivity.reason: A generalisation about baalei teshuva: that without proper instruction they easily end up "not human", impossible to talk to.
sensitivity.publishable: A person whose whole approach to religion is *emuna*, with a passionate drive for altruism, can easily end up not being a person without proper instruction. Connect that to one aspect of the truth and he becomes forcefully attached to it, and he is not going to be human. You cannot sit down and talk to him: he is on a holy mission, and if you try to talk to him, he is not there.

blocks.text: Say something they do not want to hear and they get angry, and try to put you down, even insult you, to invalidate your opinion; whether by invalidating you or the thing itself, they do not care. They already know it is bad, so it does not matter how they get it away from you; they are not considering what you say. It is not healthy, and not comfortable to be around.

sensitivity.reason: Continues the generalisation about baalei teshuva who were not properly instructed.
sensitivity.publishable: Say something he does not want to hear and he gets angry, and tries to put you down, even insult you, to invalidate your opinion; whether by invalidating you or the thing itself, he does not care. He already knows it is bad; he is not considering what you say. It is not a healthy thing, not comfortable to be around.

blocks.text: So that is not a person. A person sees a deeper will and how all these *ratzonos* fit, and so can see the other's point of view: I may think that practically, by a *ratzon murkav*, this is better, but I can understand him, and I also have a will for that.

Like the Baal Shem Tov's saying: if you see a bad in somebody else, you really have it in yourself. Anything you see in another you have in yourself in some way; every person really has all these *ratzonos*.

blocks.title: The truth, and the lower realms
blocks.text: Often there are fights because people lock onto two essential wills when inwardly they want the same thing. Take *emuna* and making a *dira b'tachtonim* (a dwelling below): taking the full truth of *Yiddishkeit* and bringing it down into the world, into the lower realms. One locks onto one side: "If it's going to be a *dira b'tachtonim*, you can't dilute the truth." The other locks onto its having to be in the lower realms.

It is like one person in the lights and vessels of *Tohu*, another in the lights and vessels of *Tikun*. One lets go of the real goal just to compromise; another keeps his goal but will never accomplish it, because he will not compromise on how. Some are very altruistic but not practical, some are practical. Really your goal is to bring it out, so you have to do both.

phrases.he: אלא בבחינת התיקון, דוקא
phrases.en: the *inyan* of a person is *davka* in a way of *Tikun*,

phrases.he: שכל נקודה בא בהתפשטות חוץ מעצמיותה,
שאז מתכללים על ידי ריבוי הכלים מכלים שונים שמורכבים בהם כו'
phrases.en: when it comes out from the *etzem hanekuda* into *Tikun*, then all the opposite things are expressed, but they're expressed in a limited way, kind of.

phrases.he: ודי למבין

blocks.title: From the yeshiva to mivtzaim
blocks.text: Rather, only in *Tikun*, when every *nekuda* comes out into *hispashtus*, outside its essence: **the *inyan* of a person is *davka* in a way of *Tikun***. You do not let the *nekuda* stay in its altruism. A teenager sitting in *yeshiva* can easily be altruistic; out on *mivtzaim* (outreach) you have to be practical. You cannot tell someone you want to bring up, "Well, religion is an all-or-nothing thing. If you believe in Judaism, then you have to do everything it says." That is really the truth: if this is what G-d wants, I will do everything. But practically, a person cannot start doing everything.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 opens with the first half of line 46 (w0-59), read without the alignment's mark, which falls on the second half at w1201.

blocks.text: It is the same *mashal* we used for the *igulim*: the *igulim* are the way it is in hiddenness, and this is the way it comes out, revealed, in a particular thing. They correspond; the difference is only whether it is the essence or already for a particular.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: That is what a person needs to bring it into *Tikun*, to make *hishtalshelus* (the chain of descent). He does not drop the essential thing; he writes it on a piece of paper, puts it in his pocket, and asks what his practical goal is. If he really wants what *Hashem* wants, a baby step he can actually do is not hypocritical: it is the only way he will ever do it.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: The *yetzer hara* gets a person to say, "No, I want to do everything. If I'm going to do it, I'm going to do it right, I'm going to be perfect." Why the *yetzer hara*? Because it comes from *Tohu*, from all or nothing.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: From the *chesed* of *Tohu* you say, "I have an essential connection to G-d. No matter what I do, G-d's going to be with me and He's going to love me, so it doesn't matter what I do." That can come out to *kelipa* (what conceals G-dliness): the *chesed* of *Tohu* becomes the root of the *kelipa* of Yishmael.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: The *gevura* of *Tohu* says, "No matter what I do, I'm never going to be able to act in a way that's good enough" for G-d, never do the *mitzvos* perfectly, never express in action the full glory He deserves: "there is no righteous man on earth." So: "If I'm never going to be perfect, there's always room to improve, so then what's the point of ever starting?"
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: And this is the root of the *kelipa* of Esav, a *gevura* of *kelipa*. He does not know much about the Muslim philosophy, "but Christianity, this is what they say": G-d wants you to do the Torah and the *mitzvos*, but you cannot do them without sinning, without messing up somewhere, so you need not do any of them; just rely on being saved by "Yoshke". So from the *gevura* of *kelipa* came out a kind of *chesed*: "Well, you can just do whatever you want, really." They are so *gevura*-dik by nature that they give up.

sensitivity.reason: Describes Christian teaching on the commandments disparagingly and names its founder with a derogatory Yiddish nickname.
sensitivity.publishable: And this is the root of the *kelipa* of Esav, a *gevura* of *kelipa*. A person says: G-d wants you to do the Torah and the *mitzvos*, but you cannot do them without sinning, without messing up somewhere, so you need not do any of them. So from the *gevura* of *kelipa* came out a kind of *chesed*: "Well, you can just do whatever you want, really." He is so *gevura*-dik by nature that he gives up.

blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: This is what the *yetzer hara* does: it makes a person altruistic, kind of, locked into one of these essential *middos*, until it becomes debilitating, a lack of action. That is a *ratzo* (running towards) without a *shov* (returning): a *ratzo* for the *Tohu*, which is good, but no focus on the result.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: Focused on the result, wanting it to come down in practice, you ask, "How can I use this *chesed* of good to motivate me to do good?" Like this: however low I am, there is always some meaningful step I can take, and I have value. A person feels lifted up: G-d treasures him, and his little effort is worth as much to G-d as a big *tzaddik*'s (righteous person's), because it is on his level. That is how it comes into holiness.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: And the *gevura* side: no matter how much I have accomplished, I can never be happy with it, because there is always room to improve. That is how Yitzchak and Yaakov used *chesed* and *gevura*. The difference is whether you are focused on the bottom line, what you actually accomplish. If you are, it is of *Tikun*, a good thing; otherwise it is *Tohu*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: Then they are revealed through the many vessels, the different vessels compounded in them: **when it comes out from the *etzem hanekuda* into *Tikun*, then all the opposite things are expressed, but they're expressed in a limited way, kind of**. You find a place for each. That is a *partzuf*: all are expressed together because each is limited to one example, and so you can have them all together.

phrases.he: וזה מה שכתוב בספר יצירה
טרף אש ומים ובללן זה בזה
phrases.en: Take *eish u'mayim* and mix them together.

phrases.he: דהיינו בחינת המורכב דאש ומים דוקא, ולא בעצם מהותן כו' וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר באריכות:

blocks.text: And this is what *Sefer Yetzira* (the Book of Formation) says: **Take *eish u'mayim* and mix them together**; that is how *Hashem* made the world. Essential fire and essential water are opposites, physically and spiritually, but an actual physical world needed those forms combined. No physical thing is purely fire or purely water, and the same spiritually.

That is, the composite of fire and water *davka* (specifically), not their very essence, as explained elsewhere at length. In physical things you cannot have one without the other: nothing is completely, externally perfect, and nothing has no merit. You always have both.

reviewQuestions.question: What does it mean that each *sefira* of *Tohu* is a *nekuda*, and why does dividing each *sefira* into ten make *Tikun*?
Why is the person who reads Dale Carnegie's book not *chafetz chesed*, and what does the essential will for kindness have that his will lacks?
Why can two opposite essential wills not compromise, and what happens to the person who is "totally nice, always" or who says "get it yourself"?
Why could Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel not convince each other, and why is their dispute only half an example?
How is kindness to one who saved your life different from the kindness of a person who is kind by nature?
How could G-d punish Shaul and order his eulogy at the same time, and what does that show about the composite *middos* of *Tikun*?

Shaul and the Givonim (74 w1151-1346): he says Shaul killed the Givonim "because they helped Dovid". In the verses (Shmuel II 21) the plague is for Shaul's killing of the Givonim; the link to helping Dovid comes through the city of Nov, whose kohanim gave Dovid food and whom the Givonim served (a Midrashic reading). The block keeps his words; a reviewer may want to check.
"Where His judgement is, there..." (74 w1106): he says he forgets the end of the verse; the block keeps it as an unfinished quotation.

"That's the way that Yitzchak and Yaakov used chesed and gevura" (76 w1138-1150): kept as he said it, though chesed and gevura are usually paired with Avraham and Yitzchak. A reviewer may want to check whether he misspoke. The next sentence's "the ratzui of Tikun" (76 w1173-1185) is unclear in the transcript and is rendered only as "it is of Tikun".

"The long short way and the short long way" (73 w1638-1776): he tells it without naming the source; it is the Gemara's story (Eruvin 53b) of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and a child at a crossroads, which he retells as a way to a palace. Kept as he tells it.

"One person in the lights of Tohu and the vessels of Tohu, one in the lights of Tikun and the vessels of Tikun" (75 w2183-2220): kept as he said it; the pairing with the two people that follow (the one who compromises the goal and the one who will not compromise the means) is not spelled out, and he may have meant lights of Tohu in vessels of Tikun.
